newsitem.title: USA: IBM employee buyout plan seen Thursday.
newsitem.headline: IBM employee buyout plan seen Thursday.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp is expected to announce an anticipated voluntary buyout plan to its eligible employees Thursday, to rebalance its workforce and redeploy its resources, sources said.
A spokesman for the Armonk, N.Y.-based computer giant declined to comment.
The buyout plan is likely to be aimed at U.S. employees in non-strategic and support functions at many U.S. locations. IBM is not expected to disclose the number of staff targeted.
But analysts said that the move is aimed at getting 6,000 to 10,000 employees worldwide out of its slower growth areas.

"The goal is to get as many people as possible to take it," said one industry source who asked not to be identified. "This is the unwritten text, when you offer this if you don't take the carrot, you know the stick is back there and do you risk waiting for the stick."

The "stick" refers to the possibilty of layoffs, analysts said, if not enough employees decide to take the buyout offer. Others may also be offered jobs at IBM's faster growing units, such as its services business, which has added about 10,000 staff this year with plans to add 4,000-5,000 more before year end.

"Look at how efficient it is to manufacture (the newer) CMOS mainframes versus the water cooled bipolar models," Jones added. "You don't need the personnel to manufacture those products anymore. There is a natural reduction in head count."

The buyout plan will likely entail one week of pay for every six months of employment at IBM with a ceiling of six months, analysts speculated. Only certain employees, such as having been employed over five years, are eligible.
Analysts do not expect a charge for this buyout plan, because IBM has told analysts to include $800 million for restructuring costs into their financial models this year.

But if not enough employees take the plan, layoffs are very possible before the end of the year, analysts and sources said. As one possible inducement for employees, IBM considered raising its age for full retirement benefits, from 55 now to 60 or 62, but sources said that plan was dropped for now.
"You can bet that in November, IBM will be back saying we didn't get enough people to leave voluntarily," one source said. "They will have to sweeten the offer or lay off people."
At the end of 1995, IBM had a total worldwide workforce of 225,000, with 110,000 of those employees in the U.S. U.S. employment is expected to grow as IBM adds to services.
"If you are not selling it, if you are not making it and you are not designing it, then what are you doing? Watch out," said Sam Albert, a Scarsdale, N.Y.-based consultant.

While sources said that IBM is only targeting the U.S. "infrastructure" staff with this buyout plan, analysts said that they believe there are several slower growth areas of its business where IBM could trim its staff, such as maintenance, bipolar mainframe manufacturing, storage division and some European areas where it is difficult to lay off workers.
"You just look at the mainframe business," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst.
